study.title: Acts 3 - Healing, testimony, and call to repentance
study.overview: In this chapter, Peter and John go up to the temple and find a lame man of birth, whose healing happens publicly, immediately and undeniable in the name of Jesus Christ. The miracle does not end in admiration: he opens space for the preaching of Peter, who diverts all the attention of the apostles to Jesus, the Holy and Righteous, dead, risen and glorified by God. The sermon interprets healing as a sign of Jesus" power and calls Israel to repentance, conversion and listening to the promised Prophet. The chapter concludes by showing that the promises made to the parents achieve their fulfillment in Christ, who comes first to the people of the covenant to bless him, turning him away from his wickedness.

outline.title: The healing of the lame man and the reaction of the people
outline.explanation: Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer and find a man who was brought daily to ask for alms. Instead of money, heals in the name of Jesus Christ, with instant restoration of the ability to walk. Man enters the temple praising God, and the people, recognizing him, is surprised and amazed.

outline.title: Peter explains that the miracle points to Jesus
outline.explanation: Before the crowd, Peter rejects any idea of the apostles' own power. He attributes the healing to the God of the patriarchs, who glorified Jesus, whom the people delivered, denied and killed. At the same time, he states that Christ's death did not frustrate the purpose of God, but fulfilled what the prophets had announced.

outline.title: Called to repentance and fulfillment of promises
outline.explanation: Peter calls on the people to repentance and conversion, promising forgiveness, refreshment and restoration from the presence of the Lord. He presents Jesus as the Prophet announced by Moses and witnessed by the prophets. Finally, it shows that the blessing promised to Abraham first comes to the children of the covenant, in order to turn them away from wickedness.

study.context: The chapter shows Peter and John going to the temple at the time of prayer, which places the episode within the religious life of Israel and the public practice of piety. The healed man was known to all for being daily at the door of the temple asking for almsgiving; this makes the miracle publicly verifiable. The meeting takes place in a space of great circulation, including the porch called Solomon, where the crowd meets after the sign. Peter's speech appeals to the Scriptures of Israel - Moses, Samuel, the prophets, and the promise made to Abraham, indicating that the apostolic message is a continuation of the previous biblical testimony.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that apostolic signs do not point to the messengers, but to Jesus Christ, whose person and name express authority and power. The healing of the lame man functions as a visible sign that the risen continues to act among his people. Theologically, Peter connects the cross to divine sovereignty: the rejection of Jesus was real human sin, but also fulfillment of the purpose announced in the Scriptures. The answer required is repentance and conversion, no mere religious admiration. The blessing promised by God is not just foreign or political; it includes forgiveness, renewal, and separation from sin. The promise to Abraham is seen as directed to the good of all the families of the earth, showing that God's mission is neither selfish nor restricted.

scholarViews.insight: The name of Jesus represents his identity and his power to heal; therefore, healing does not come from Peter, but from the authority of Christ.
Peter takes advantage of popular admiration for the miracle to preach Christ, diverting the honor of the apostles to the Lord and explaining the sign to the light of the gospel.
The mission of Jesus is first addressed to the people of the covenant, so that they may be blessed by being removed from their iniquities; the blessing promised to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ.

questions: When God uses me in some spiritual good, is my first reaction to direct glory to Christ or seek recognition for me?
Does my idea of blessing be limited to external benefits, or does it include repentance, forgiveness, and withdrawal from sin?
Do I read the death and resurrection of Jesus as historical chance, or as a fulfillment of God's plan announced in the Scriptures?
study.practice: This week, when realizing any response from God to his prayer or any opportunity to serve, practice two gestures: first, explicitly thank Jesus instead of assigning merit; second, examine a concrete area of wickedness, confess it before God and take a practical step of detachment from it. It is also worth using Acts 3 as a model of evangelistic conversation: to begin with what God did in Christ, to explain the biblical meaning and to call repentance with clarity and meekness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the focus of the chapter on Jesus, repentance and the fulfillment of the biblical promises, but do not fully detail the archaeological or historical identification of the door called Formosa nor allow to accurately develop all the chronological elements of the hour of prayer. There are also small differences of emphasis between the commentators, especially on how to explain the relationship between Christ's suffering and God's sovereign purpose; here they were presented as interpretations, not as incontestable conclusions.
